chapter.title: What it owes: debts, soon and later

cards.body: You owe the bank $200,000 and the plumber $400. Which one is knocking on your door this Friday? In the house picture, the mortgage gets paid a slice a month for 25 years, but the plumber wants paying now. A balance sheet sorts debts the same way, because **when a debt is due matters more than how big it is.**
cards.simpler: You owe the bank $200,000 and the plumber $400. Which one will knock on your door this Friday? With a house, you pay the mortgage a bit each month for 25 years. The plumber wants paying now. A balance sheet sorts what a company owes in the same way, because **when a debt is due matters more than how big it is.**

cards.prompt: Mo has a flat with a $180,000 mortgage and 22 years left to pay. Mo also has a $900 credit card bill due on the 28th, and $60 in the bank. Which debt is the problem this month?

options.text: The card bill. It's due in days and $60 can't cover it.
Neither. The flat is worth more than both debts put together.

whyNot.a: That's the biggest debt, not the most urgent one: only this month's slice of the mortgage is due, not the full $180,000.
whyNot.c: That's what Mo owns, not what Mo can pay with: the card company won't take a bedroom by the 28th.

cards.reteach: A debt starts to hurt when it comes due, not when it's big. The $900 lands in days and Mo has $60, so that's the squeeze. The mortgage gets paid in small slices over 22 years.

cards.title: Soon: current liabilities
cards.body:
*Current liabilities* are everything the company has to pay within 12 months of the date on the balance sheet. Picture the envelopes on the doormat: the gas bill, the card statement, the plumber's invoice.

On a real sheet they have names like *accounts payable* (bills from suppliers that haven't been paid yet), *short-term borrowings* (loans due within the year) and *taxes payable* (tax owed but not paid yet).

**This is the pile that has to be paid in real cash, soon.** Each line also tells you who's waiting at the door: a supplier, a bank or the tax office.
cards.simpler: *Current liabilities* are everything a company must pay within 12 months of the date on its balance sheet. Think of the bills on your doormat. On a real sheet you'll see *accounts payable* (unpaid bills from suppliers), *short-term borrowings* (loans due within the year) and *taxes payable* (tax owed but not yet paid). **This is the pile that must be paid in real cash, soon.** Each line shows who is waiting: a supplier, a bank or the tax office.

cards.title: Rosa's bakery, 31 December
cards.body:
Rosa's bakery has a balance sheet dated 31 December. Current liabilities: $6,000 owed to the flour supplier, $4,000 of sales tax owed to the tax office, and the $2,000 of the van loan that's due next year. Total: $12,000.

Long-term liabilities: the other $18,000 of the van loan, plus a $40,000 bank loan due in 2031. Rosa owes $70,000 in all, but only $12,000 of it has to be paid by next December. The flour supplier is owed less than a tenth of the total, and will still be the first to call.
cards.simpler: Rosa's bakery has a balance sheet dated 31 December. Current liabilities: $6,000 to the flour supplier, $4,000 of sales tax and $2,000 of the van loan, making $12,000. Long-term: the other $18,000 of the van loan and a $40,000 bank loan due in 2031. Rosa owes $70,000, but **only $12,000 must be paid by next December**. The flour supplier is owed under a tenth of the total, yet will call first.

cards.prompt: A bike shop's balance sheet is dated 30 June 2026. Which of these goes under current liabilities?

options.text: A bank loan that has to be paid back in full in March 2029.
$3,000 owed to a tyre supplier, due in 30 days.

whyNot.a: That's long-term, not current: March 2029 is more than 12 months after 30 June 2026.
whyNot.c: That's something the shop owns, not something it owes: the van is an asset, on the other side of the sheet.

cards.reteach: Current means due within 12 months of the date at the top. Count one year forward from 30 June 2026: anything owed before 30 June 2027 is current. The tyre bill is due in 30 days, so it counts.

cards.title: Later, and the slice that moves
cards.body:
*Long-term liabilities* are debts due more than 12 months away: a 10-year bank loan, *bonds* (IOUs a company sells to investors), a long lease on a building. In the house picture, this is the mortgage. It's big, but you pay it a slice at a time.

You'd think a loan stays in one place. It doesn't. Rosa's van loan sat on both sides: the slice due this year moved up into current liabilities, often called the *current portion of long-term debt*.

**A long-term loan turns current as its due date gets closer.** A loan that looked harmless last year can be top of the pile this year.
cards.simpler: *Long-term liabilities* are debts due more than 12 months away: a 10-year bank loan, *bonds* (IOUs a company sells to investors), or a long building lease. Think of a mortgage: big, but paid a bit at a time. A loan doesn't stay put, though. The part of Rosa's van loan due this year moved up into current liabilities, called the *current portion of long-term debt*. **A long-term loan turns current as its due date gets closer.**

cards.body: Priya opens a company's balance sheet, sees "Long-term debt: $0" and relaxes. Then she spots "Short-term borrowings: $5 million" under current liabilities, due this year, while the company has $1 million in the bank. Last year that same loan was listed as long-term. It hadn't been paid off; it had come due. Always read the current liabilities first, then the long-term ones.
cards.simpler: Priya opens a company's balance sheet, sees "Long-term debt: $0" and relaxes. Then she spots "Short-term borrowings: $5 million" under current liabilities, due this year. The company has only $1 million in the bank. Last year that same loan was listed as long-term. It wasn't paid off. It had come due. **Always read the current liabilities first**, then the long-term ones.

cards.prompt: A friend says: "This company owes $50 million, so it's in trouble." What should you check first?

options.text: How much of the $50 million is due in the next 12 months.
Whether $50 million is more than the company's yearly sales.
How many different banks the money is owed to.

whyNot.b: That compares debt to sales, which is a different question: first you need to know when the $50 million is due.
whyNot.c: That's who it owes, not when: one lender or ten, the danger is how much has to be paid this year.

cards.reteach: The total tells you how much is owed. The split tells you how soon. $50 million due in 2035 is like a mortgage; $50 million due by Christmas is a pile of bills on the doormat.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A balance sheet splits what a company owes into two piles: current liabilities, due within 12 months, and long-term liabilities, due later. **The total tells you how much; the split tells you how soon**, and debts coming due soon are what sink companies.

Tomorrow: how a business can be worth less than nothing and keep running.
cards.simpler:
A balance sheet splits what a company owes into two piles. Current liabilities are due within 12 months. Long-term liabilities are due later. **The total tells you how much; the split tells you how soon.** It's the debts due soon that sink companies.

Tomorrow: how a business can be worth less than nothing and keep running.

cards.body: Search for a company you know plus "balance sheet" and find "Total current liabilities". Write down that number and the date at the top. That's what it has to pay before the same date next year.
cards.simpler: Search online for a company you know plus "balance sheet". Find the line that says "Total current liabilities". Write down that number, and the date at the top of the sheet. **That's what the company has to pay before the same date next year.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now list what a company must pay in the next 12 months, what it can pay later, and who it owes.
